As someone who has spent years of their life playing the franchise modes in Madden and NBA 2K, this is the game I've been looking for. The level of depth is absolutely unparalleled. It makes the manager modes in other games look pitiful in comparison.

I've never been a soccer fan. In fact, I'd say I actively disliked soccer in the past, which is why I've always been hesitant to try this game. I decided to give it a shot however, and I've been missing out so hard. Not only on the game (it's great though), but on the sport itself, as well.

This game has made me a soccer fan. I'm going to my first soccer game this weekend, so thanks I guess.

Was really tossing up buying the game as didn't have any particular saves planned. Have 1000+ hours on FM21 (and similar numbers for FM18/20) and thought that the game didn't look different enough from the previews. I was shocked when I played the game and noticed so many new features/UI updates. The data analysis update makes the analytics easier to understand and provides more precise information on how you your players/team follows your tactics, its even really fun just going through in depth and finding hidden details. In terms of gameplay, I don't have a great understanding of the engine, but my first reactions are it looks more and more like your team is actually playing football and its not just the same 8 or so different highlight packages that FM can often feel like. The Centre Backs is where I've noticed the greatest difference, not just with the new Wide Centre Back role (which is a lot of fun to mess around with) but even with Ball Playing Defenders actually making runs forward like you'd see in a real game and not just mulling round on the ball before launching a long ball into space. Finally if you like doing the small stuff like attending press conferences and team talks, the dialogue feels a lot more randomized/unique this year (so far). Overall, if you love FM, 22 provides so much more than just a roster update, and you're bound to notice the subtle changes in details that make all the difference.

It's 2051. LOSC Lille are playing in the final of the Coupe de France, a competition they haven't won for 4 decades. 5 years ago, they were in Ligue 2. Yet here they are, in the final of a major competition after so long. It's tied, 0-0. The opposition, perennial title contenders Olympique Lyonnais, had dominated the match up until star midfielder Alexandru-Mihai got sent off in the 69th minute. Since then, it's been in deadlock, no side offering much offensively. LOSC striker Koutan gets a strike chalked off in the 84th for offside, and now it's in extra time. It passes quickly, no chances either side. That is, until the 119th minute of 120.

Pierre Gicquel was born in Lille in 2033. For all his 17 years, he'd loved the club. His parents recalled the glory days of the club to him, culminating in title glory in 2021. His entire life, he'd dreamed of being the one to restore his club to greatness, to have the captain's armband while carrying the team to national, even worldwide, glory. From a young age, the staff at LOSC knew he was special, even being touted as the next Kylian Mbappe. Small, a mere 5'7, but incredibly agile, he started out as a striker but quickly found his place as a winger. He tore up every youth division he played in. Now, here he is, 17 and it's his first professional season for the club. Gicquel has played a big part in the team's first title challenge since 2021, but to start the cup final, he was on the bench.

With the minutes winding down in extra time, LOSC's Dutch winger Ibrahim Jabbie was exhausted, and there was an obvious choice waiting in the wings. Gicquel stepped on the pitch, and if the weight of a city was on his shoulders, he didn't show it. 

It's the 119th minute. There's 1 minute of added time. It's the last attack of the game. Gicquel and right-back Balek are exchanging passes on the wing. Suddenly, a hole appears. Gicquel sees it, and swiftly dodges inside before the defenders can react. He cuts to the edge of the box. He's on his weaker left foot. He doesn't care. He's 25 yards out. He doesn't care. All he cares about is this city, this stadium, the one he grew up in the shadow of. The stadium whose visitors now all stare at him in awe. This club, the one he's been sitting in front of the TV, watching, supporting, following, for every day of his life. 

Pierre Gicquel strikes the ball. Everyone in the building knows where it's going. Top corner. Completely unsaveable.

Gicquel became a LOSC legend that day. Everyone knows that someday he might grow up, he might leave, he might even force his way out. None of that matters. On one sunny day in May 2051, football was the winner, and Gicquel was its vessel. Perhaps it's just a game. But in that fateful moment, that game changed lives, and gave the world a story to be told for generations to come.

Been playing FM for about 15 years and as always it is a great game and i'll always get several hundred hours out of the game as a minimum, but please for love of god like I have said every year for the last 5 update the UI & UX.

The game itself is superb It is so cluttered, and the graphical parts of the game are more fitting of 2011, not 2021. The regen & manager faces are still awful (despite Miles wearing them as some sort of badge of honor - they look terrible) and the backgrounds on the stadiums just ruin any visual aspect of the game. Neither of those would take huge amounts of resources to improve but make a massive difference. There is a huge modding community (that SI continues to make life difficult for) that do a much better job than SI and they all do it for free anyway.

As for the menus, they are 5 years out of date - there are several things you have to go through many menus to get too when 1 click would do a job. It would not hurt them to strip it back and make the menus simpler, and group the information inside that. For several years now they have just added new features ontop of the current menus and it makes them cluttered and unorganised. I would be happy if FM23 consisted of absolutely no improvements, just a major UI / UX redesign, it would make such a difference. 

The little gripes: The price range feature is stupid and once again just adds more layers to an already cluttered UI/game. It just gives you more information than you need.

The squad/transfer menus are so buggy and haven't changed for 10 years, anybody that has tried to create their own squad/transfer view will know what I am talking about. It is like it's only mini game inside the game just trying to rearrange the views. 

Overall the game is superb and the best football game by a long way, but it is starting to feel like a game where they have added 10 years of updates on top of a game, instead of making a new game. The game is cluttered and you have too much information that you just don't need. A proper UI/UX redesign next year please SI.

FM is now FIFA. It's clear that SI are investing as little development into each edition as they can get away with. Comments elsewhere have suggested that the fair solution (for gamers) would be releasing a patch every season with an update of players rather than a whole new game. As can be seen, I've given plenty of hours to this edition so I think it's fair to say that these observations are based on a significant amount of experience with the game. 

1) Transfers. With each edition, this gets more and more skewed in favour of the AI. You will rarely if ever sell a player for close to their valuation, yet any attempts to purchase an AI player for less will be rejected. The loan system is even worse, with negotiations only possible on your loanees, not on an AIs. 

2) ME. The match engine hasn't improved and with every patch, something changes to ruin your previously developed tactic. There was a brief moment when FM22 came out that strikers finished one on ones, but that was clearly too realistic for SI so that was 'fixed'. Also good luck defending against the inevitable 30 yard effort from the opposition player who hasn't scored all season...

3) Other: The game is riddled with annoying little flaws; the board scores are ridiculous, the inability to negotiate objectives is infuriating and a backwards step from previous versions... don't even get me started on the "dynamic youth rating"! 

In conclusion, I don't feel I can recommend this game anymore. I've had every edition since the switch to FM and it is without a doubt that there has been little actual improvement in the way the game plays. Yes, there's been "new features", though the usefulness of the analysis is dubious given the inevitability of some of the match engine gameplay. Unless FM23 offers a radical overhaul and massive improvement in the areas above, I think my time playing this game is over and that is one of the saddest realisations a gamer can have!

Dabbled in FM13 back in the day, moved to FM21 last year and never really got my head wrapped around the insane playtime of the people playing it. Fast forward to FM22 and the loss of time is real. I don't consider myself an avid fan of the sport (or sports at all) but digging your heels in and really focusing on the inner workings of a football club has hooked me more than I thought it would. Every win feels like you put the work in and every loss hurts at an emotional level. Sure you can click through and hope you win, but the real meat is spending the time reading the reports, analyzing not only your team but your upcoming opponents, keeping your ear to the ground for club info around the league, and so much more. The addition of the data hub has allowed someone who isn't very knowledgeable of the sport to get a concise view of my strengths and shortcomings in a very easy to digest manner. I feel like my understanding of the game grows with every day that passes for my club. 

I am obviously ill-equipped to comment on the caliber of changes from previous iterations but much like yearly sports titles, if you are consistently buying these at every release you will have a much different view than I do when it comes to it's level of change and how well it's received. 

In short, for someone who isn't a die hard "fan" of football, this is great way to learn the game and the simulation level of interaction caters to the more OCD side of my personality. I'd encourage anyone with even a passing interest of sports management to take a look at FM22. Even if you aren't a sports nut, you'll find something to love here if you don't mind taking your time to learn how the majority of this game has little to do with what happens directly on the pitch. There is a whole world running between matches that includes finances, player personalities, building beneficial relationships, scouting, managing injuries, training, etc. that dictate how well you are able to perform as a club. While it is overwhelming for the newcomer, there are endless resources online to guide you to your next victory or emotionally shattering loss.

If I was to compare this game to FM21...

+ The introduction of the Data Hub provides a better way of judging whether your tactic is working, comparing your players with the rest of the league, and analysing the opposition.
+ Dynamic youth ratings are huge for long-term build-a-nation saves, as the quality of youth players will change depending on the nation's standing.
+ Scouting regions have been split up, allowing you to assign scouts to more specific areas of a continent.

- Avatar customisation looks to have gotten worse. The beards are laughably bad, and look like they were done using the airbrush in MS Paint.

If you have a mind for analytics, like to do build-a-nation saves, or just want the database update, I would absolutely recommend picking up FM22. If you only use plug-and-play tactics, are a casual player, and/or are tight for cash, then maybe stick with FM21 as it is still a good game.

As an avid FM player for the past seven editions, I am sad to say that this is by far the worst FM I've ever played. It feels like this is a buggy early beta build, not a fully released product. The match engine is the most unrealistic so far, with the only viable tactics in most situations being some form of pressing, short passing system even in lower leagues where this type of tactic shouldn't be possible. No matter what happens, even the worst teams in the league have completion percentages of 85% or higher, which if you know anything about football you'd recognize as being a bit absurd (maybe that would be normal for the best teams, but when the worst team in the sixth tier of English football is passing with 90% accuracy, you know something is wrong). Sometimes defenders decide to just wander off and are nowhere near the play. You can't play with anything other than a high defensive line, as crosses are way too effective this year. The transfer system is a bit of a mess, with players complaining about asking prices even when the interface says they should be happy with the asking price. I've had players throw a tantrum about their price being too high when a dozen teams were willing to meet it and the agent said it should be fine. Expected playing time vs accurate playing time is glitched, and sometimes the player who has started each of the dozen league games you've played so far will complain because the game thinks they're only being used as a squad player. Then there's features like "dynamic youth rating" which were misrepresented by SI (youth rating doesn't actually change except for very rare circumstances), who then give snappy responses when called out on it. SI's reaction as a whole to any criticism of the game or reports of bugs usually boil down to "not a bug, you just don't like our game being realistic", even when it's clearly an unrealistic bug, which is disappointing coming from a developer who is usually very good about interacting with the game's community. If SI would have re-released FM2018 with updated squads and called it FM2022 I would recommend it in a heartbeat, but I just can't recommend this game as is. If you really want to simulate last season, buy FM21 and download one of the third-party roster updates, but skip FM22 and hope that they do a better job with FM23.

I've been playing football managing games since 1995 (Ultimate Soccer Manager, PC Fútbol, Championship Manager, Total Club Manager and many others). Since 2014 I've been pretty much settled with the FM franchise, I've been playing Football Manager 2015 for the past 7 years, and after giving FM2022 a shot I think I will simply continue playing FM2015 for another 5 years at least.

[b]I do not understand how is it possible that Sigames keeps simply UIwashing the same exact game[/b], with the same exact issues, and selling it for €55 season after season, even though it's been a while since they don't even have to pay for FIFA and UEFA licenses because someone will just mod them out for them.

I believe the match engine hasn't improved a bit in 7 years, besides tiny adjustments in the animations. The training system is still quite annoying, so I just skipped it and delegated it to my coaches. The tactics are exactly the same as they were in 2014, with really minor changes, and they still have the same issues. They assume, for instance, tikitaka style must be played pushing the game through the center of the field, while in reality Barça and the Spanish team always used open wingers and really tried to make the field as wide as possible. Because of that, if you want to succeed in this game, you have to go for Italian catenaccio and counterattack or for a Premier League direct attacking style.

[b]The press conferences were already annoying in FM2015, and they are even worse now[/b]. Sure, they have more options now, but that only means you waste more time reading the new questions and answers and picking the ones that you will be repeating forever from that moment on. Plus, you now have a second press conference after every match. [b]Another thing that you will most likely delegate to your coaches[/b].

There are even several aspects where I find the game is worse than FM2015. [b]Contracts are a nightmare. There is no room for negotiation whatsoever[/b], players have their demands and you must meet them or they will leave. Plus, their demands often make no sense. [b]I've had several players asking for 20M yearly salary contracts, which I denied, and then they signed for different clubs for just 10M[/b]. Rookies ask for insane amounts of money or protagonism. One of my rookies, 17, refused to even discuss his new contract because I refused sending him on loan to a 2nd division team six months earlier, while he was playing regularly and won the triplet twice with my team. My team, by the way, is the richest and is at the top of the ranks in prestige. [b]Truly seems like the constant whining of the players is just another way Sigames has found to make players spend more hours playing[/b], just like the exhausting press conferences and so on, but there is really nothing pleasant in negotiations or discussions with players whatsoever.

[b]I'm truly sad there is no real competition for this game to actually push some improvement on it[/b]. Sure, it's a very good game, it was 10 years ago. But it's still the same now, almost exactly the same as it already was in 2011. How is it possible that this franchise keeps charging €55 for every single UI rewashing, and how is it possible that everyone keeps buying it year after year? That is simply beyond my understanding.

Football Manager is a stellar series of games and '22 is no different. There have been massive updates to the match engine and it's beginning to feel more and more realistic with each year. 

There are some problems with it though. The dynamics/player interactions system is completely screwed. Players will get angry at the littlest of things, and often you are walking a tight rope when interacting with your players. The transfer-list value is completely screwed, and your players will come to you if you offer them out for even the most minute discrepancies in value. Keeping your players happy while also winning is far more difficult than it should be. This area of the game is more like a dating sim than a football sim.

In the same boat, the transfers this year seem like a complete toss up. It really feels like it's down to luck trying to either sell players for their value or get players for a fair value. Loans seem to be near impossible to secure without a senior affiliate. 

The staff meetings are completely useless. All they've done is taken what used to be a single email and put it in a long step-by-step meeting thing that takes far longer than it needs to. If you like to get really involved in the game, often times they will suggest things that aren't helpful or opposite to what you're trying to do (i.e. get a player to train a completely different skillset to what you need). 

The same goes for the transfer window meetings. I'd personally rather it just come up in the scouting email.

For each thing I dislike about the game there's about 100 I love, so take these with a grain of salt. But this year the improvements outside of the match engine don't really feel like improvements at all.

It's still definitely worth buying and a lot of fun.

I play FM a decent amount, I've played a few past iterations a decent amount, I watch a decent amount of FM videos on Youtube (shoutout to Zealand) and I actually really enjoy it. 
Last year's engine I thought was a little too exploitable but i figured this year it would be better. I haven't poured a lot of hours into the game yet, but I feel like certain tactical layouts are not as easy to set up to make unreasonably overpowered tactics (I haven't tested a lot though, wait for the actual pros to whip out some 150 goals a season tactics and I'll take all my nice words back).
I won't talk about the match engine as I'm sure many players, possibly more skilled at recognizing problems with it than me, have already said plenty about it (although I feel like I have to mention one thing, please please please fix my wingers and fullbacks. I don't know why, but when my team starts a counter attack, 1 time in 5 my fullbacks and wingers will just straight up dribble the ball out of bounds to the sideline with NOBODY pressing them.)
What I have to address, for the love of football, is how many unreasonable measures are implemented into the game to make it harder.
I'll be the first to agree that once you've got an effective tactic going, your players are in shape, you've made a few good purchases with a solid scouting network and sold a few wonderkids for decent money, the game does start getting easier than I'd like and honestly expect, especially since you can decently transform a team in two seasons if you know what you're doing (without exploiting game mechanics).
But the measures implemented into the game to try to prevent this from happening are total nonsense.
I'll just list one very very glaringly obvious example but there's unfortunately quite a few more.

Buying and selling players:
Can you get a few wonderkids for cheap here and there? Yes, granted you've scouted them. (I don't like looking up high potential, cheap, young players online as that ruins the experience for me).
What makes no sense is why a player that is wanted by absolutely nobody, gets an offer from me outside of a transfer window, the transfer story doesn't leak (or not that I'm notified of), a week later he still hasn't accepted my contract offer, I think it's suspiscious and go check and I find out that in the meantime even Jesus Christ put a bid on that player.
I adapt my contract offer, offering more money and better playing time, giving him a contract that realistically makes little sense for a player of his calibre but I do it anyway cause I really want him. The player accepts my new offer during negotiations again. A week later still nothing, and then I find out he's gone to a WEAKER team in the SAME championship for LESS money!? Fine, maybe he's been rooting for that team ever since he was a kid (although I doubt an Argentine wonderkid grew up watching Bologna play, but I digress).
Not to mention the requests you get from clubs and players alike during transfers, which are also completely unreasonable. I'll have to pay 10 mil for the transfer of an okay player, 3mil€ a season plus bonus in the contract, whilst I'm managing a modest Serie A side whose best player barely gets 3mil WITH bonuses. I'll break down transfer talks as I deem the requests unreasonable, two weeks later that same player goes to a similar team in a transfer deal worth 5mil with a contract of 2 mil a season.
Wanna make managing the transfer market harder? I'm all for it. Go ahead and make training dynamics more complicated and fragile for newly purchased players, adding a new layer of decision making as to whether a player might develop well once he's been bought; make agents play a bigger role in negotiations as they manipulate their clients; give family members a role in transfers too; heck, give the option to monitor how secretly a transfer deal is being managed with possible countermeasures such as salary fees for all the staff involved in negotiations if there's a leak, but DON'T make the game harder through completely irrational scenarios (or mysteriously guaranteed injuries two days before ANY big match).

I played all the FM games except for FM 18-19 and FM 21. Fm 17 was a big no-no for me in terms of how similar it played out to the previous games and, I decided not to buy 18 and 19. Fm 22 is a HUGE improvement to any other FM games I've played, especially FM 20. This game is a drug and I'll probably dump another 1000 hours into it because I'm a hopeless addict. But I'm not happy with the direction Football Manager has been going in with the past few versions.

I recently fired up FM17 out of curiosity, and found the experience so much more streamlined. No more meetings that could have been emails. No more performance evaluations with the owners about whether I'd signed enough Portuguese players. No more forcing the latest updates from the Canadian Premier League down my throat by automatically going to the News and Around The World pages. Less staff members with vague titles whose jobs I don't understand. No more debriefings after meetings telling me "Actually players don't like being yelled at." FM17 ran faster, so less downtime waiting for the game to process. FM17 allowed me to focus on the core engagements of the game - trying to fit tactics to teams, finding and signing talent, developing players, and a reasonable amount of man management. FM22 is certainly more realistic. But that realism looks suspiciously like an actual job.

There are aspects of FM22 that I missed. Dynamic youth rating is definitely an intriguing feature, even if its implementation is contentious (I think it was correctly implemented, but clearly some people disagree). The player valuation system and transfer market is much improved. I do like that player development is more variable, even if in the moment it's frustrating when the wonderkid I'd put all my hope in doesn't turn out. All these require a level of adaptability previous versions of FM just didn't ask of you. And while FM17's five year old database is a fun nostalgia trip, at some point I'll want to return to present day. I very well may return to FM22. Certainly nothing is a total deal breaker with it. But it's become clear that SI have built a bloated mess with a terrible UX and it's really tempered my enthusiasm for this franchise I've been playing for the last decade.

The new Data Hub is a useful feature for those who like to track data statistics for performances, the team, and individual players. Really helps you pinpoint where your team/players do well and where the weaknesses are. Also makes better use of your analysts. The match engine is marginally better but still seeing players just gliding on the pitch. The layout for the scouting centre and coach reports is an improvement, although the coach report is no longer showing how a player compares to others in that position like it used to. Estimated player valuations add a bit more realism, rather than having a set value there is now a range which will hopefully reduce the number of cases where a club tries to negotiate for £100m on a player valued at £20m (for example).

Might as well play a slot machine. Your tactics don't matter. Attributes don't matter. It's all convoluted and vague, maybe even pre-scripted to ensure a realistic football experience.  However, when I play a video game I want some resemblence of agency. I want to know that my actions actually matter. I want to see my instructions translate into something, anything, on the field; and Football Manager fails to offer that time after time. 

If you're into the all realistic football experience than by all means this is a great game. If you want to have fun, look elsewhere.

+New details and feature (e.g. data hub with stats and data like xG and xA that tend to confuse you till you go read/Google it out).
